57.title: The search
57.hook: monkeys sent in four directions; Sampati the vulture's news
57.howItsDone: The search for Sita and Sampati's news are told in Ramayana readings and recitations; the scene leads straight into the Sundara Kanda, Hanuman's leap to Lanka, which is often recited on its own.

segments.voice: Last time: chaturmas, four months of rain and a hero who couldn't move. Waiting is a season.

A lost set of keys. The whole house turned upside down. Then a grandmother, without getting up from her chair, asks: did you check your coat? Hold on to that. The rains end, and Sugriva, now king and comfortable, has half forgotten his promise. Lakshmana storms into the monkey city so angry the walls seem to shake, and it takes Tara, the wise queen, to calm him down. Then Sugriva moves fast. He sends his whole army out in four great search parties: north, east, west and south. One month, he says. Search every mountain, every forest, every cave. And he gives Hanuman, heading south, Rama's ring.
screen: `THE RAINS END.` → `LAKSHMANA STORMS IN.` → `FOUR ARMIES, FOUR DIRECTIONS.` → `HANUMAN GETS THE RING.`

segments.voice: The northern, eastern and western parties come home with nothing. The southern party, with Hanuman and young Angada, Vali's son, finds nothing either. They get lost in an enchanted cave. The month runs out. They sit down on the shore of the ocean, at the very tip of the land, and give up. Going home empty-handed feels impossible, so, in Valmiki's telling, they decide to fast there until they die. As they talk, Angada mentions Jatayu, the old bird who died fighting Ravana. And a voice answers from the cliffs. An enormous, ancient vulture with no wings has heard the name. It's Sampati, Jatayu's older brother. Long ago, he says, the two brothers raced toward the sun, and when Jatayu flew too close, Sampati spread his wings over him, and his own wings burned away. He's been stuck on this cliff ever since, and he hadn't heard his brother was dead until now. Then Sampati gives them what a whole army couldn't find. A vulture's eyes see very far, he says. I can see her. Across the ocean, a hundred yojanas away, in the city of Lanka, sits Sita. And as he speaks, in the story, new wings begin to grow. Notice where the answer came from. Not from running harder, but from an old, broken bird on a cliff, the one nobody thought to ask, and because someone spoke with love about his brother. His news sends Hanuman to the ocean's edge, and to the great leap you already know.
screen: `THE MONTH RUNS OUT.` · `A VOICE FROM THE CLIFF: SAMPATI.` · `HE BURNED HIS WINGS FOR HIS BROTHER.` · `I CAN SEE HER: LANKA.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've been searching for, an answer, a direction, a way through, and notice where you've been looking: online, round and round in your own head, the same three friends. Then ask: who's the old bird I haven't asked? A grandparent, a retired neighbor, someone who's been through it, someone you've written off; let a face come up, and just notice who you've been walking past.
The search. An army in four directions, a month gone, and the answer from a wingless old bird on a cliff.
Your line: ask the old bird. The answer came from the last place anyone looked. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: The bridge
58.hook: stones float; the squirrel carries sand
58.howItsDone: Rameswaram, on the Tamil Nadu coast, is an important pilgrimage place linked to the building of the bridge; the chain of shoals between India and Sri Lanka is often called Rama Setu, and the squirrel story is a favorite told to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the search, and Sampati, the wingless old vulture who could see Sita across the sea. Ask the old bird.

Hanuman has leapt the ocean, found Sita, given her the ring, and set Lanka on fire. Now he's back, and the whole army stands on India's southern shore looking at the problem. Hanuman can jump a hundred yojanas. A monkey army can't. Rama sits on the beach for three days, in Valmiki's telling, asking the ocean to let them pass. The ocean doesn't answer. So Rama, furious, picks up his bow and aims an arrow at the sea itself. And the ocean rises out of the water, in person, and says: don't dry me up. There's another way.
screen: `AN ARMY AT THE EDGE OF THE SEA.` → `THREE DAYS, NO ANSWER.` → `RAMA AIMS AT THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: The ocean god tells Rama that one of his monkeys, Nala, is the son of the builder of the gods, and can build a bridge the sea will hold up. So the army goes to work. They tear up trees, boulders and whole rocky hilltops, carry them to the water, and Nala lays them in a line. The stones float. In Valmiki it takes five days to reach Lanka. People call it Rama Setu. Setu means bridge: Rama's bridge. In later tellings, the monkeys write Rama's name on each stone, and that's why they float. And then there's the squirrel. You won't find it in Valmiki; it comes from later tellings, especially popular in the south. While the monkeys haul boulders, a little squirrel runs down to the water, rolls in it, rolls in the sand up the beach, and runs back to shake the sand off between the stones. Over and over. A monkey laughs at it, or nearly steps on it. What are you doing, tiny thing? Rama picks the squirrel up and says its work matters: it's filling the gaps the big stones leave. And he strokes its back with three fingers. Look at the Indian palm squirrel: three pale stripes down its back. That, people say, is where Rama touched it. The story puts the two side by side. A giant project isn't only boulders. It's also the sand that keeps the boulders from wobbling. The big contributions are easy to see; the small ones hold them together. And whoever notices the squirrel is paying attention the way Rama does.
screen: `NALA, SON OF THE GODS' BUILDER.` · `THE STONES FLOAT: RAMA SETU.` · `A SQUIRREL CARRIES SAND.` · `THREE STRIPES WHERE RAMA TOUCHED IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something big you're part of, a family, a team, a school, a neighborhood, the work of looking after someone, and find your part in it that nobody sees: the dishes, the check-in text, the thing you fix without being asked. Don't measure it against the boulders; let the sand you've been carrying count. Then bring to mind someone else's small part you've never thanked.
Rama Setu. Rama's bridge: floating stones across the sea to Lanka, with a squirrel filling the gaps.
Your line: the squirrel counts. Sand is what keeps the stones still. Tomorrow, Ravana's court.

59.title: Angada in the court
59.hook: the young prince's foot no one can lift
59.howItsDone: Angada's foot in Ravana's court is a favorite scene of the Ramlila plays of north India, often played for both drama and laughter, and it is recited from the Lanka Kand of Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama Setu, the bridge of floating stones, and a squirrel filling the gaps. The squirrel counts.

A meeting where everyone's against you. A family dinner where you're the one they've decided to blame. A new school, first day, the whole table looking at you. The army has crossed the bridge. Before the war starts, Rama sends one last messenger into Ravana's court, to give the king a chance to return Sita and avoid the fighting. Not Hanuman, who already burned the place down. Angada. Young. Vali's son, the prince whose father Rama killed. And Angada walks alone into a golden hall full of demons, and faces the king with ten heads.
screen: `A ROOM THAT'S AGAINST YOU.` → `ONE LAST CHANCE FOR PEACE.` → `ANGADA WALKS IN ALONE.`

segments.voice: Ravana knows Angada's father died by Rama's arrow, and tries to use it: why serve the man who killed your father? Join me. It's a good move, and Angada doesn't take it. His father, dying, asked Rama to look after him, and he has chosen his side. The most famous version of this scene comes from the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi Ramayana of Tulsidas, the one most people in north India know. Angada delivers Rama's words, and the court mocks him. So he does something strange. He plants one foot on the floor and says: if anyone here can move my foot, Rama will turn back and give up Sita. The court laughs. Then, one by one, Ravana's great warriors grab his foot and heave. It doesn't move. Not an inch. The laughing stops. Finally Ravana himself gets up from his throne and bends to grab it. And Angada pulls his foot away and says, in effect: why hold my feet? If you want to be saved, go and hold Rama's feet. In Valmiki's older telling the scene is different: Angada speaks for Rama, the demons seize him, and he leaps up, breaks through the palace roof, and flies back. Both versions agree on the core. A young man alone, in the most hostile room in the world, stays steady and says exactly what he came to say. The foot is a picture of that. You can't move someone who knows why they're standing there.
screen: `RAVANA TRIES TO TURN HIM.` · `ONE FOOT ON THE FLOOR.` · `NOBODY CAN MOVE IT.` · `GO AND HOLD RAMA'S FEET.`

segments.voice: Put both feet flat on the floor and feel the ground pushing back. Picture a room you'll walk into soon where you'll feel outnumbered, and before you speak in it, feel your feet and remember, in one sentence, what you came to say. You don't need to win or be loud; just stay where you are, and breathe into your feet.
Angada, Vali's son, a young prince alone among enemies, who plants a foot in Ravana's court that nobody can lift.
Your line: plant your foot. Steady isn't the same as loud, or the same as winning. That's fifty-nine.

60.title: Vibhishana crosses
60.hook: Ravana's brother chooses the other side
60.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors Vibhishana as a devotee of Rama and one of the long-lived ones of tradition, and Rama's promise of refuge to him is often recited as a verse of assurance; the Hindi proverb about 'the insider bringing down Lanka' shows the other way people remember him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angada in Ravana's court, the young prince whose foot nobody could lift. Plant your foot.

A family dinner where everyone agrees about something that's wrong, heads nodding around the table, and one person who can't nod along. The story rewinds a little, to a scene Valmiki puts before the bridge. Inside Lanka, Ravana calls his council. Monkeys are gathering on the far shore. What should we do? One after another, his generals and ministers say: we'll crush them, great king. Then his younger brother stands up. Vibhishana. And he says the thing nobody in that golden room wants to hear.
screen: `THE ONLY ONE WHO SAYS IT.` → `RAVANA'S COUNCIL OF WAR.` → `HIS BROTHER STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: Give Sita back, Vibhishana tells his brother. Taking her was wrong, and it will destroy Lanka. Make peace with Rama. He says it once, carefully, then again. And Ravana explodes. He calls his brother a traitor and a disgrace to the family, and in some tellings, including Tulsidas's, kicks him in front of the whole court. So Vibhishana makes a choice people still argue about. He rises into the air with four companions, crosses the sea, and hovers above Rama's camp. I'm Ravana's brother, he calls down. I've left everything. I've come for refuge. The monkeys are sure it's a trick, and Sugriva says kill him. Rama says no. In Valmiki's telling, Rama says it's his vow: anyone who comes to him even once asking for shelter, saying I am yours, he will protect, from anything. Even, he adds, if it were Ravana himself. Then, before a single battle, on the beach, Rama has Vibhishana anointed as the future king of Lanka. The tradition holds him two ways. Devotees revere Vibhishana as a great devotee who chose dharma over family. And an old Hindi saying uses him the other way, roughly: the insider brings down Lanka. Traitor or conscience, the story makes you look at both. What it's clear about is this: he spoke first. He told the truth inside the room twice before he ever walked out of it. Leaving wasn't his first move. It was his last.
screen: `GIVE HER BACK, HE SAYS. TWICE.` · `RAVANA CALLS HIM A TRAITOR.` · `ANYONE WHO COMES FOR REFUGE.` · `CONSCIENCE, OR TRAITOR?`

segments.voice: Think of a room that was bad for you, a group chat, a friendship, a job, a habit of talking about people, and look, with no judgment, at whether you ever said the true thing inside it. Then think of a room you're in now that isn't right: what would it sound like to say the true thing once, calmly, and if nothing changed, where's the door?
Vibhishana crosses. Ravana's younger brother, who told the truth twice and then walked over to Rama's side.
Your line: walk across. Rama's door stayed open, even to Ravana's brother. Sixty days now.

61.title: The first battle
61.howItsDone: The war in Lanka is staged over several nights in the Ramlila plays of north India that lead up to Dussehra; some readers take the battle both as a story and as a picture of the inner struggle to stay steady.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhishana crosses, the brother who told the truth twice and then walked over. Walk across.

Some nights the noise doesn't stop. The neighbors are fighting, the baby won't sleep, your phone keeps lighting up, your own head won't quiet down. Lanka, now, is that loud. A golden city on a mountain, ringed with walls and moats, four great gates, each guarded by an army. Outside, on the plain, a sea of monkeys and bears, and two princes with bows. The talking is over. Angada's embassy failed. Vibhishana has told Rama where every gate is. At dawn, the monkeys rush the walls, climbing, hurling rocks and trees. And the fighting doesn't stop when the sun goes down.
screen: `THE GOLDEN CITY, WALLED.` → `FOUR GATES, FOUR ARMIES.` → `THE MONKEYS RUSH THE WALLS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki's war books are long, loud and crowded. Duel after duel: monkey against demon, champion against champion, names you'll never need to remember. The first day's fighting runs into the night, and that's when it gets frightening. The demons of Lanka are said to grow stronger in the dark. Nobody can see who's friend and who's enemy. Valmiki describes a terrible darkness filled with shouting, the clash of weapons, cries in the dark, rivers of blood. The monkeys lash out at shadows; some fight their own side by mistake. And in the middle of the chaos, the story keeps putting one image in front of us: Rama, steady. Arrows come from every side, and he answers them calmly, one at a time, as if the noise isn't touching him. Under the story runs a second one. A battle isn't only outside. The noise gets in, the fear gets in, the confusion gets in, and you start swinging at shadows. The Gita, which comes later on this path, has a word for the person who stays level in pleasure and pain, in noise and quiet: sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still. Rama, in this scene, is a picture of that. Not someone who's escaped the fight. Someone in the middle of it, still inside. The walls of Lanka won't fall for a long time; this is the first night of many. And already the question is not only who wins, but who can stay steady until morning.
screen: `THE FIGHTING RUNS INTO THE NIGHT.` · `IN THE DARK, SWINGING AT SHADOWS.` · `RAMA, STEADY, ONE ARROW AT A TIME.` · `STHITAPRAJNA: WISDOM THAT STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Don't try to make it quiet: let whatever noise is around you, traffic, voices, a hum, a fan, be there, and find your breath underneath it. Each time a sound grabs you, or your own mind is the noisy one, notice it and come back to one breath. You're not winning against the noise; you're staying level in it.
Sthitaprajna, the one whose wisdom stands still in pleasure and pain. Lanka's first battle runs into the dark, and one warrior stays steady inside it.
Your line: still, inside. The first night in Lanka is long, and morning is far off. Steady, till tomorrow.

62.title: Indrajit's illusion
62.hook: the fake Sita killed before the army
62.howItsDone: Teachers in Advaita Vedanta often use the rope-and-snake example when explaining maya; the illusory Sita scene is told in Ramayana readings as a picture of despair built on a false image.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sthitaprajna, the wisdom that stands still, and Rama steady in a battle that ran into the dark.

A video lands in the group chat and stomachs drop. Hours later it turns out to be fake, but by then it's been felt, believed and shared. Ravana's son has a name that means conqueror of Indra, king of the gods: Indrajit. He's one of Lanka's fiercest warriors, and his weapon isn't only arrows. It's illusion. He fights invisible, from inside the clouds. Early in the war, his arrows turn into snakes and bind Rama and Lakshmana so tight they fall as if dead. Now he tries something crueler. He rides out in his chariot in front of the whole monkey army, and beside him sits Sita.
screen: `A FAKE VIDEO, A REAL FEELING.` → `INDRAJIT: CONQUEROR OF INDRA.` → `SITA, IN HIS CHARIOT.`

segments.voice: Thin, grieving, in a dirty robe, exactly the Sita Hanuman found in the garden. Hanuman freezes. As the whole army watches, Indrajit grabs her by the hair, raises his sword, and kills her. The monkeys scatter in despair. What was the point of any of it? Hanuman runs to Rama with the news, and Rama collapses. Then Vibhishana, who knows his family, stops everything. Think, he says. Ravana would never allow Sita to be killed. It's maya: a conjured image. My nephew made a Sita out of illusion to break your heart, so you'd stop fighting while he performs a ritual that would make him unbeatable. He's right. The Sita in the chariot was never Sita. Maya is a big Sanskrit word. In everyday speech it can mean magic, trickery, illusion. In Hindu philosophy it grows much bigger: the power that makes things appear other than they are. Teachers of the Advaita tradition use a famous picture for it. In the half-dark, you see a coiled rope on the ground and jump back, heart racing: snake! Your fear is completely real. The snake never was. When the light comes, it's just rope. Advaita teachers use it to talk about the whole world and the self; other Hindu schools understand maya differently, and they'll come later on the path. Today, it's enough to see what the story sees. Indrajit's weapon was never the sword. It was the image, and the despair it caused. The way out wasn't more fighting. It was someone calmly saying: look again.
screen: `SITA IN THE CHARIOT, KILLED.` · `LOOK AGAIN, SAYS VIBHISHANA.` · `MAYA: THINGS APPEARING OTHERWISE.` · `SNAKE IN THE DARK. ROPE IN THE LIGHT.`

Then hold something scaring you now, without arguing with it, and ask gently: is this a snake, or is it rope, and is there someone who could help me look again?

Your line: rope. The fear was real, and the snake never was. Day sixty-two, done.

63.title: Lakshmana falls
63.hook: the arrow; the herb; Hanuman flies
63.howItsDone: Images of Hanuman flying with the mountain in one hand are familiar in Hindu homes and temples, and devotees pray to him as sankat mochan, remover of troubles, especially on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's illusion, the false Sita, and Vibhishana's calm voice: it's maya, look again.

In the thick of the fighting, a weapon strikes Lakshmana full in the chest. In Valmiki's telling it's a great spear flung by Ravana himself. It's the blow that almost ends the story, after a week of wonders: an old bird on a cliff, a bridge of floating stones and a squirrel, Angada's foot, Vibhishana walking across, a night battle in the dark, a false Sita. Lakshmana, who followed his brother into exile without being asked, falls, and doesn't get up. Rama drops to the ground beside him. And the whole army is asking: who can get there in time?
screen: `A SPEAR STRIKES LAKSHMANA.` → `A WEEK: CLIFF, BRIDGE, FOOT, NIGHT.` → `WHO CAN GET THERE IN TIME?`

segments.voice: You heard this story from Hanuman's side a few weeks ago: the mountain of herbs. Today, sit on the other side of it, on the ground with Rama. The man who faced armies without flinching holds his brother's head in his lap and comes apart. What do I want with victory, he says, in effect, what do I want with Sita, even, if Lakshmana is gone? Then a line that is hard to hear: a wife can be found again, and friends and kin anywhere, but where in the world would I find a brother like this one? It isn't a ranking of love. It's grief talking, the way grief does. Then the physician of the monkey army, Sushena, kneels and looks. He's not dead yet, Sushena says. There are healing herbs on a mountain far to the north, near the Himalaya. One is called sanjivani, the herb that brings back life. In the telling Tulsidas gives, they have to be here before dawn. The Himalaya is the length of India away. And Hanuman simply goes. He doesn't debate it or ask whether it's possible. He flies. When he can't tell which glowing plant is which, he lifts the whole peak and carries it back, and Lakshmana breathes and stands up. The story holds something on both sides of that flight: grief that's allowed to be total, even in a hero, and a friend who doesn't calculate. The distance was impossible. He flew anyway. Devotees call Hanuman sankat mochan, remover of troubles, and this is the kind of night they mean.
screen: `RAMA ON THE GROUND WITH HIS BROTHER.` · `WHERE WOULD I FIND A BROTHER LIKE THIS?` · `SANJIVANI, BEFORE DAWN.` · `HANUMAN DOESN'T DEBATE. HE FLIES.`

segments.voice: Think of a time you were on the ground, a night in a hospital, a phone call that changed everything, and see the face of whoever drove across the city at two in the morning, stayed on the phone for hours, or just came. Let yourself feel what it meant. Then turn it around: is there someone, far away or close, whose Hanuman you could be?
Lakshmana falls. The brother who followed Rama everywhere, struck down, and the friend who flew the length of India before dawn.
Your line: fly. A friend doesn't measure the distance. That's the week, and day sixty-three.
